{{Short description|Matrices satisfying a differential equation}}
In [[mathematics]], in the theory of [[integrable system]]s, a '''Lax pair''' is a pair of time-dependent matrices or [[operator (mathematics)|operator]]s that satisfy a corresponding [[differential equation]], called the ''Lax equation''. Lax pairs were introduced by [[Peter Lax]] to discuss [[soliton]]s in [[continuous media]]. The [[inverse scattering transform]] makes use of the Lax equations to solve such systems.

==Definition==
A Lax pair is a pair of matrices or operators <math>L(t), P(t)</math> dependent on time, acting on a fixed [[Hilbert space]], and satisfying '''Lax's equation''':

: <math>\frac{dL}{dt} = [P, L],</math>

where <math>[P, L] = PL - LP</math> is the [[commutator]].
Often, as in the example below, <math>P</math> depends on <math>L</math> in a prescribed way, so this is a nonlinear equation for <math>L</math> as a function of <math>t</math>.

==Isospectral property==
It can then be shown that the [[eigenvalue]]s and more generally the [[Operator spectrum|spectrum]] of ''L'' are independent of ''t''. The matrices/operators ''L'' are said to be ''[[isospectral]]'' as <math>t</math> varies.

The core observation is that the matrices <math>L(t)</math> are all similar by virtue of

: <math>L(t) = U(t, s) L(s) U(t, s)^{-1},</math>

where <math>U(t, s)</math> is the solution of the [[Cauchy problem]]

: <math>\frac{d}{dt} U(t, s) = P(t) U(t, s), \quad U(s, s) = I,</math>

where ''I'' denotes the identity matrix. Note that if ''P''(''t'') is [[skew-adjoint]], ''U''(''t'',&nbsp;''s'') will be [[unitary operator|unitary]].

In other words, to solve the eigenvalue problem ''Lψ'' = ''λψ'' at time ''t'', it is possible to solve the same problem at time 0, where ''L'' is generally known better, and to propagate the solution with the following formulas:
: <math>\lambda(t) = \lambda(0)</math>&emsp;(no change in spectrum),
: <math>\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = P \psi.</math>

=== Through principal invariants ===
{{See also|Invariants of tensors}}
The result can also be shown using the invariants <math>\operatorname{tr}(L^n)</math> for any <math>n</math>. These satisfy 
<math display=block>
 \frac{d}{dt} \operatorname{tr}(L^n) = 0
</math>
due to the Lax equation, and since the [[characteristic polynomial]] can be written in terms of these traces, the spectrum is preserved by the flow.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hitchin |first1=N. J. |author-link=Nigel Hitchin |title=Integrable systems : twistors, loop groups, and Riemann surfaces |date=1999 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=Oxford |isbn=0198504217}}</ref>

=== Link with the inverse scattering method ===
The above property is the basis for the inverse scattering method. In this method, ''L'' and ''P'' act on a [[functional space]] (thus ''ψ'' = ''ψ''(''t'',&nbsp;''x'')) and depend on an unknown function ''u''(''t'',&nbsp;''x'') which is to be determined. It is generally assumed that ''u''(0,&nbsp;''x'') is known, and that ''P'' does not depend on ''u'' in the scattering region where <math>\|x\| \to \infty.</math>
The method then takes the following form:
# Compute the spectrum of <math>L(0)</math>, giving <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\psi(0, x).</math>
# In the scattering region where <math>P</math> is known, propagate <math>\psi</math> in time by using <math>\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t}(t, x) = P \psi(t, x)</math> with initial condition <math>\psi(0, x).</math>
# Knowing <math>\psi</math> in the scattering region, compute <math>L(t)</math> and/or <math>u(t, x).</math>

=== Spectral curve ===
If the Lax matrix additionally depends analytically on a complex parameter <math>z</math> (as is the case for, say, [[sine-Gordon]]), and the deformation is isospectral, the equation
<math display = block>
 \det\big(wI - L(z)\big) = 0,
</math>
defines an analytic subset of <math>\mathbb{C}^2</math> with coordinates <math>w, z,</math> which under suitable hypotheses is a curve, often after removing singularities. By the isospectral property, this curve is preserved under time translation. This is called the '''spectral curve''', often after taking a suitable compactification. When the dependence of ''L'' on ''z'' is algebraic, it is an [[algebraic curve]]. Such curves appear in the theory of [[Hitchin system]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hitchin |first1=N. J. |title=Integrable systems : twistors, loop groups, and Riemann surfaces |date=1999 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=Oxford |isbn=9780198504214}}</ref>

== Zero-curvature representation ==
Any PDE which admits a Lax-pair representation also admits a zero-curvature representation.<ref name="SIT">{{cite book |last1=Dunajski |first1=Maciej |title=Solitons, instantons, and twistors |date=2010 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-857063-9 |pages=54–56}}</ref> In fact, the zero-curvature representation is more general and for other integrable PDEs, such as the [[sine-Gordon equation]], the Lax pair refers to matrices that satisfy the zero-curvature equation rather than the Lax equation. Furthermore, the zero-curvature representation makes the link between integrable systems and geometry manifest, culminating in [[Richard S. Ward|Ward]]'s programme to formulate known integrable systems as solutions to the [[Yang–Mills equations|anti-self-dual Yang–Mills]] (ASDYM) equations.

=== Zero-curvature equation ===
The zero-curvature equations are described by a pair of matrix-valued functions <math>A_x(x, t), A_t(x, t),</math> where the subscripts denote coordinate indices rather than derivatives. Often the <math>(x, t)</math> dependence is through a single scalar function <math>\varphi(x, t)</math> and its derivatives. The zero-curvature equation is then
<math display=block>
 \partial_t A_x - \partial_x A_t + [A_x, A_t] = 0.
</math>
It is so called as it corresponds to the vanishing of the [[curvature form|curvature tensor]], which in this case is <math>F_{\mu\nu} = [\partial_\mu - A_\mu, \partial_\nu - A_\nu] = -\partial_\mu A_\nu + \partial_\nu A_\mu + [A_\mu, A_\nu]</math>. This differs from the conventional expression by some minus signs, which are ultimately unimportant.

=== Lax pair to zero-curvature ===
For an eigensolution to the Lax operator <math>L</math>, one has
<math display=block>
 L\psi = \lambda \psi, \psi_t + A\psi = 0.
</math>
If we instead enforce these, together with time independence of <math>\lambda</math>, instead the Lax equation arises as a consistency equation for an overdetermined system.

The Lax pair <math>(L, P)</math> can be used to define the connection components <math>(A_x, A_t)</math>. When a PDE admits a zero-curvature representation but not a Lax equation representation, the connection components <math>(A_x, A_t)</math> are referred to as the Lax pair, and the connection as a Lax connection.

== Examples ==
=== Korteweg–de Vries equation ===
The [[Korteweg–de Vries equation]] 
: <math>u_t = 6uu_x - u_{xxx}</math>
can be reformulated as the Lax equation
: <math>L_t = [P, L]</math>
with
: <math>L = -\partial_x^2 + u</math> (a [[Sturm–Liouville operator]]),
: <math>P = -4\partial_x^3 + 6u\partial_x + 3u_x,</math>
where all derivatives act on all objects to the right. This accounts for the infinite number of [[first integrals]] of the KdV equation.

=== Kovalevskaya top ===
The previous example used an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Examples are also possible with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. These include [[Kovalevskaya top]] and the generalization to include an electric field <math>\vec{h}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bobenko |first1=A. I. |last2=Reyman |first2=A. G. |last3=Semenov-Tian-Shansky |first3=M. A. |date=1989 |title=The Kowalewski top 99 years later: a Lax pair, generalizations and explicit solutions |url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1104178400 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |volume=122 |issue=2 |pages=321–354 |issn=0010-3616 |bibcode=1989CMaPh.122..321B |doi=10.1007/BF01257419 |s2cid=121752578 }}</ref>

: <math>\begin{align}
L &= \begin{pmatrix}
g_1 + h_2 & g_2 + h_1 & g_3 & h_3\\
g_2 + h_1 & -g_1 + h_2 & h_3 & -g_3\\
g_3 & h_3 & -g_1 - h_2 & g_2 - h_1\\
h_3 & -g_3 & g_2 - h_1 & g_1 + h_2\\
\end{pmatrix} \lambda^{-1}\\
&+ \begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & -l_2 & -l_1\\
0 & 0 & l_1 & -l_2\\
l_2 & -l_1 & -2 \lambda & -2 l_3 \\
l_1 & l_2 & 2 l_3 & 2 \lambda\\
\end{pmatrix},
\\
P &= \frac{-1}{2} \begin{pmatrix}
0 & -2 l_3 & l_2 & l_1\\
2 l_3 & 0 & -l_1 & l_2\\
-l_2 & l_1 & 2 \lambda & 2 l_3 + \gamma\\
-l_1 & -l_2 & -2 l_3 & -2\lambda\\
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}</math>

=== Heisenberg picture ===

In the [[Heisenberg picture]] of [[quantum mechanics]], an [[observable]] {{mvar|A}} without explicit time {{mvar|t}} dependence satisfies

: <math>\frac{d}{dt} A(t) = \frac{i}{\hbar} [H, A(t)],</math>

with {{mvar|H}} the [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] and {{mvar|ħ}} the reduced [[Planck constant]]. Aside from a factor, observables (without explicit time dependence) in this picture can thus be seen to form Lax pairs together with the Hamiltonian. The [[Schrödinger picture]] is then interpreted as the alternative expression in terms of isospectral evolution of these observables.

===Further examples===
Further examples of systems of equations that can be formulated as a Lax pair include:

* [[Benjamin–Ono equation]]
* One-dimensional cubic [[non-linear Schrödinger equation]]
* [[Davey–Stewartson equation|Davey–Stewartson system]]
* Integrable systems with contact Lax pairs<ref>A. Sergyeyev, New integrable (3+1)-dimensional systems and contact geometry, Lett. Math. Phys. 108 (2018), no. 2, 359-376, {{arXiv|1401.2122}} {{doi|10.1007/s11005-017-1013-4}}</ref>
* [[Kadomtsev–Petviashvili equation]]
* [[Korteweg–de Vries equation]]
* [[KdV hierarchy]]
* [[Marchenko equation]]
* [[Modified Korteweg–de Vries equation]]
* [[Sine-Gordon equation]]
* [[Toda lattice]]
* [[Lagrange, Euler, and Kovalevskaya tops]]
* [[Belinski–Zakharov transform]], in general relativity.

The last is remarkable, as it implies that both the [[Schwarzschild metric]] and the [[Kerr metric]] can be understood as solitons.

==== Discrete time dynamics ====
The concept of Lax pair can also be defined for [[Dynamical system#Discrete dynamical system|dynamical systems with discrete time]], for instance the [[Pentagram map#The spectral curve|pentagram map]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=WEINREICH |first=MAX H. |date=2022-11-25 |title=The algebraic dynamics of the pentagram map |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/etds.2022.82 |journal=Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems |volume=43 |issue=10 |pages= |at=§5 The Lax representation |doi=10.1017/etds.2022.82 |issn=0143-3857|doi-access=free }}</ref>
